prompt: The card was chosen because it has the three parts every framework has to answer for. Which three?
hint: What changes, what follows it, and what draws both.

choices.text: A router, a store and a test
choices.why: Those are parts of an application, and the card has none of them: it is one component and an entry file.

choices.text: Props in, events out, and a slot for the content
choices.why: That is how components talk to each other, which the card never does: it is mounted on its own.

choices.text: State, derived values and a template
choices.why: Right. The sessions change, the two totals follow them, and the template draws both and sends the tick back.

choices.text: A component, a build and a dev server
choices.why: Each version does have those, but they are the project around the card, not the parts of it the comparison reads.

prompt: The Vue card starts with the 19 October session done. After the 23 October one was ticked, how many minutes did it say were done?
hint: 30 minutes, plus 40.

prompt: The Vue console printed `Vue: setup runs` once, before the tick and not after it. What did the tick do instead?
hint: Lessons 2 and 3: a reactive list, and what reads it.

choices.text: It ran the setup again quietly, without its log
choices.why: Nothing reran the setup: the log is its first line, so a second run would have printed it again.

choices.text: It had Vite reload the module, which kept the old totals
choices.why: Vite reloads a module when a file is saved, not when a box is ticked, and the totals did change, to 70 of 70.

choices.text: It replaced the whole list with a copy
choices.why: That is React's way and Angular's. `v-model` changed `s.done` inside the reactive list, with no copy.

choices.text: It changed `s.done`, the two `computed`s were marked stale, and only the parts of the template that use them were redrawn
choices.why: Right. That is the whole model in one line of console: the setup builds the connections once, and a change reruns what read it.

prompt: Before the tick, `React: WeekCard runs` appeared twice. Why twice?
hint: Look at what `main.tsx` wraps the card in.

choices.text: `<StrictMode>` calls it a second time, in development, on purpose
choices.why: Right. It brings out code that is not safe to run more than once; a production build calls it once.

choices.text: The card has two sessions, and the function is called once per session
choices.why: The function is the whole card; the sessions are drawn by `.map` inside one call.

choices.text: Vite's dev server loads the module once to connect and once to draw
choices.why: `[vite] connecting...` came before both lines, and Vue's and Svelte's cards, on the same server, ran once.

choices.text: Once to draw the list and once more to work out the two totals
choices.why: The totals are plain `const`s inside the same call; working them out is not a separate run.

prompt: How does the React card's `toggle` mark a session done?
hint: Lesson 3's `toggleDone`.

choices.text: It sets `s.done` on the list `useState` returned, and React sees the field change
choices.why: React does not watch inside the value: changing a field of the old list would draw nothing new.

choices.text: The input writes `s.done` itself, through `checked`
choices.why: `checked` only draws the state; the change is asked for by `onChange`, which calls `toggle`.

choices.text: It builds a new list with `map` and hands it to `setSessions`
choices.why: Right. React draws again because it was given a new value.

choices.text: It calls `useMemo` so that the two totals are worked out again
choices.why: The card never uses `useMemo`; the totals are recomputed because the whole function runs again.

prompt: Which of these are true of the React card? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare each with the four points the lesson lists against the Vue card.

choices.text: The totals are plain `const`s, worked out again every time the function runs
choices.why: Right. Nothing caches them unless you ask with `useMemo`.

choices.text: The markup is a template that the build reads beside the function
choices.why: There are no templates in React. The markup is JSX, inside the function, turned into function calls.

choices.text: The checkbox is controlled, `checked` drawing the state and `onChange` asking for the change
choices.why: Right. With no `v-model`, both directions are written out.

choices.text: The totals are cached between runs, as Vue's `computed`s are
choices.why: That would need `useMemo`, which the card does without: for a sum of two numbers nobody should ask for it.

choices.text: Each `<li>` drawn by `sessions.map` carries a `key`
choices.why: Right. The same `key` as `v-for`'s, for the same reason.

prompt: React keeps a derived value from being worked out again on every run only when asked, with `___`. For a sum of two numbers, the lesson says nobody should ask.
hint: A hook whose name says it remembers.

prompt: In the Angular card, how does the template read the `sessions` signal?
hint: Look at the `@for` line.

choices.text: With `.value`, as a `ref` is read
choices.why: That is Vue's spelling. A signal is a close kin of a `ref`, but it is read differently.

choices.text: Through `.get()`, the counterpart of `.set`
choices.why: The card changes the signal with `.update` and `.set` exists, but there is no `.get` in it.

choices.text: By calling it, `sessions()`
choices.why: Right. `this.sessions()` in the class and `sessions()` in the template, which is how Angular knows it was read.

choices.text: By its bare name, which the Angular compiler rewrites into a read
choices.why: That is closer to Svelte, whose compiler reads the runes. In Angular the read is a call.

prompt: `npm audit` offered `npm audit fix --force`. Why did the lesson set an override instead?
hint: Read the line that says what it will install.

choices.text: Half the advisories are about Windows, and the lab runs on Linux
choices.why: Some are, but others are about a cross-origin script and files served from outside the allowed folders, on any system.

choices.text: It would move `@angular/build` back to 22.1.9, older than the rest of Angular
choices.why: Right. The planner's Vite 8.3.5 already had the fixes, so pinning it everywhere fixed the audit without going backwards.

choices.text: The advisories are about the dev server, which only answers on localhost, so there was nothing to fix
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: it is the server you leave running while you browse, so localhost is no comfort.

choices.text: It would uninstall Vite, which `ng serve` needs
choices.why: The fix would have changed the version of `@angular/build`, not removed Vite.

prompt: To make every package in the Angular project get Vite 8.3.5, including the one inside `@angular/build`, the lesson ran `npm pkg set ___.vite=8.3.5`.
hint: The field of `package.json` that `npm ls` then marks with a word ending in -den.

prompt: The Angular project was made by the Angular CLI, not `create-vite`, and yet its page printed `[vite] connecting...`. Why?
hint: What is `ng serve` underneath?

choices.text: Vitest, which its `package.json` lists, opens a connection to the page
choices.why: Vitest runs tests; it was in the project, but it is not what served the page on port 4200.

choices.text: The override swapped Angular's own server for the planner's Vite
choices.why: The override changed which version of Vite was installed; Vite was already the server before it.

choices.text: `ng serve` is Vite's dev server, under Angular's own build
choices.why: Right. Which is also why the audit found a Vite inside `@angular/build`.

choices.text: The browser kept a script from the React card, served from the same port
choices.why: React's card was on port 5173 and Angular's on 4200: two origins, nothing shared.

prompt: What is Svelte, as the lesson describes it?
hint: Most of its work is done before the page is sent.

choices.text: A platform with its own CLI, router, forms and tests
choices.why: That is Angular. Svelte's project was made by `create-vite`, like Vue's and React's.

choices.text: A library that calls the component again and compares what it returns
choices.why: That is React's model. Svelte's script ran once.

choices.text: A compiler
choices.why: Right. A `.svelte` file is turned at build time into plain JavaScript that updates the page directly.

choices.text: A set of runes added on top of Vue's single-file components
choices.why: Its files look like Vue's, a script and markup, but Svelte is a framework of its own and the runes are read by its compiler.

prompt: In the Svelte card, how does ticking the box reach the list?
hint: The card has no `toggle` function at all.

choices.text: An `onchange` handler hands a new list to a setter
choices.why: That is React's shape. `$state` has no setter: changing it is an ordinary assignment.

choices.text: `bind:checked` writes `s.done` straight into the `$state` list
choices.why: Right. As Vue's reactive object did, a field inside the state is changed and seen.

choices.text: `$derived` notices the click and writes the field itself
choices.why: `$derived` is `computed`: it follows the state and never writes it.

choices.text: The `{#each}` block makes a copy of the list with the one session changed
choices.why: `{#each}` draws the list; nothing in the card copies it.

prompt: Which of these are true of the Svelte card? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three differences in kind from a Vue single-file component.

choices.text: Its state is read with `.value`, as a `ref` is
choices.why: No `.value`, no setter, no function call to read: `$state` makes a plain variable reactive.

choices.text: The markup is not inside a `<template>`
choices.why: Right. It sits in the file below the `<script>`.

choices.text: The list is a block, `{#each sessions as s (s.id)}`, with the key in brackets
choices.why: Right. Svelte's control flow is blocks.

choices.text: The totals are `$derived`, which is Svelte's `computed`
choices.why: Right. And the compiler made them signals out of the rune.

prompt: Which of the four frameworks does not track which pieces of state a computation read?
hint: The one whose console line appeared again after the tick.

choices.text: Svelte
choices.why: Svelte tracks too: its compiler makes signals out of the runes.

choices.text: Angular
choices.why: Angular tracks with signals; its constructor ran once and the tick reran what read them.

choices.text: Vue
choices.why: Vue tracks with the proxies of lesson 2.

choices.text: React
choices.why: Right. A change of state runs the whole component again, and React works out what differs in what it returned.

prompt: `useMemo` and `useCallback` exist in React, and the other three have nothing that answers to them. Why the difference?
hint: What runs again at a tick, in React and in the others?

choices.text: In React the whole function runs again on every change, so keeping some work from being redone has to be asked for
choices.why: Right. Where dependencies are tracked, only what read the changed state reruns, and there is nothing extra to keep.

choices.text: React has no other way to write a derived value
choices.why: Its derived values are plain `const`s in the function, and the card's totals worked with no hook at all.

choices.text: They stop `<StrictMode>` from calling the component twice
choices.why: StrictMode's second call is on purpose and in development only; the card was called twice with no hook to stop it.

choices.text: JSX is compiled to function calls, and those hooks make the calls cheaper
choices.why: JSX does become function calls, but the hooks are about the component running again, not about how JSX is compiled.

prompt: Built for production, how many kilobytes did the React card's JavaScript come to, gzipped? Round to the nearest kilobyte.
hint: The largest of the four.

prompt: In which of the cards does changing a field inside the state, `s.done = true`, show on the page? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where they split in two.

choices.text: Vue's, with a `ref`
choices.why: Right. The proxy sees the field change, which is what `v-model` relied on.

choices.text: React's, with `useState`
choices.why: React wants a new value: the list is copied with one session changed and handed to `setSessions`.

choices.text: Angular's, with a `signal`
choices.why: A signal notices a new value and not a change inside the old one, which is why `toggle` builds a new list in `update`.

choices.text: Svelte's, with `$state`
choices.why: Right. `bind:checked` writes `s.done` straight into the list.

prompt: Which part of the planner does the lesson call the most portable, and why?
hint: It would run unchanged in any of them.

choices.text: `CourseCard` and `SessionRow`, since all four frameworks have components with props
choices.why: The idea carries over, but the files do not: each framework writes a component in its own syntax.

choices.text: `planner.ts` and its seven tests, because they know nothing about Vue
choices.why: Right. Rules in plain functions run in any of the four, and so do their tests.

choices.text: The store, since each of the four has one
choices.why: The store library is in the list of what does not carry over.

choices.text: `vite.config.js`, since three of the four use Vite
choices.why: The lesson says lesson 17 applies to all four, but the most portable code it names is the rules, not a config file.

prompt: A student who finished this course starts the `react-ts` one. Which of these, by the lesson's account, do they bring over with almost no change? Choose all that apply.
hint: The part each framework is proud of stays behind.

choices.text: Deriving the totals instead of storing them and keeping them in step by hand
choices.why: Right. Lesson 3's rule is everyone's rule; in React the derived value is a recomputed `const`.

choices.text: The names of the lifecycle hooks
choices.why: Those are on the list of what does not carry over, with the template syntax and the store library.

choices.text: Testing pure functions first with Vitest, and faking the network and the clock
choices.why: Right. Vitest runs the tests of all four, and lesson 21 holds word for word.

choices.text: What hydration is and why a server and a browser disagree about what day it is
choices.why: Right. Next is React's Nuxt, and lesson 19's two todays happen there for the same reason.

choices.text: The exact model of what runs again when the state changes
choices.why: That is the one thing the comparison showed differs most: React reruns the whole function.

prompt: How many of the four cards ended up served by Vite's development server?
hint: Count Angular's too.

choices.text: Three: Angular has a server of its own
choices.why: `ng serve` printed `[vite] connecting...`: Angular's dev server is Vite under its own build.

choices.text: All four
choices.why: Right. Three were made by `create-vite`, and Angular's `ng serve` is Vite underneath, which is why lesson 17 applies to all of them.

choices.text: Two, Vue and Svelte, since React has a dev server of its own
choices.why: React's project was made by `create-vite` as well and printed `[vite] connecting...` like the others.

choices.text: Only Vue's, the one framework whose author also wrote Vite
choices.why: Vite is not tied to Vue: the React and Svelte templates are in `create-vite`'s own list.

prompt: Put the four cards in order of the JavaScript their production build sends, gzipped, smallest first.
hint: A compiler at one end, `react-dom` at the other.

prompt: Match each framework to the way its card draws the list of sessions.
hint: One of the spellings on the right is not any of the four.

prompt: Somebody rewrites the Angular card's `toggle` the Vue way: `this.sessions().find((s) => s.id === id)!.done = true`, with no `set` or `update`. They tick 23 October. What does the total line say?
hint: What does a signal notice?

choices.text: 70 of 70, because `computed` tracks what it read, as Vue's does
choices.why: It tracks the signal, and the signal was never given a new value, so nothing told the `computed` to run again.
Right. A signal notices a new value and not a change inside the old one: the list is the same list, so the totals stay as they were.

choices.text: 70 of 70, after the constructor runs again and recomputes
choices.why: The constructor ran once and never again, in the capture and in this case.

choices.text: Nothing: the template refuses to draw a signal changed in place
choices.why: Nothing refuses anything; the page keeps drawing, with the totals it already had.
